title: Keep Meeting Notes Close to the Decisions They Made
summary: A five-line decision block at the end of each meeting, copied into the ticket and the PR, saves the next teammate from asking why the team chose what it chose.
author: Nguyen Le Phong
html:
A new teammate opens the payment service and asks a fair question: "Why do we poll the provider every 30 seconds instead of using their webhook?" Everyone remembers there was a meeting about it. The notes are in a doc somewhere, maybe in someone's personal drive. The ticket says "Use polling." The PR says "Implements polling per discussion." Twenty minutes of Slack archaeology later, the team still can't say whether the reason was a flaky webhook, a security review or just time pressure.

The meeting did its job. The notes did too, technically. The problem is distance: the decision, its reasons and the work it changed ended up in three different places, and none of them point to each other.

Why the "why" goes missing

Michael Nygard's 2011 post on architecture decision records names the problem early: "One of the hardest things to track during the life of a project is the motivation behind certain decisions." Without that motivation, he wrote, someone new has two options: "Blindly accept the decision" or "Blindly change it" (Documenting Architecture Decisions). Neither is great. The first keeps a choice that may no longer make sense. The second undoes a choice that was protecting something nobody remembers.

Meeting notes usually fail in a specific way. They record the conversation in order: who said what, which ideas came up, where people disagreed. That's fine as a record. But the one sentence that changed the work sits in paragraph fourteen, and the reason for it is spread over paragraphs six to eleven. Six months later nobody's going to read all fourteen.

What a note needs to answer

GitLab's handbook has a good bar for this: notes "do not have to be verbatim, but they should capture key points made and be clear on any decisions or next steps" (GitLab, Live Doc Meetings). In practice that means a short block at the top or bottom of the notes that answers five questions:

Decision block

Decided: poll the provider every 30 seconds for payment status.
Why: their webhook dropped events twice during the test week, and retries aren't signed yet.
Considered: webhook only; webhook plus nightly reconciliation.
Revisit when: the provider ships signed retries (they said Q3).
Next: Linh updates PAY-412; Minh adds a dashboard for poll latency by Friday.

That's five lines. It doesn't replace the discussion above it. It just means a reader who has two minutes gets the decision, and a reader who has twenty can scroll up for the debate.

Two small habits make the block easy to write. Fill it in during the last five minutes of the meeting, while everyone's still in the room and can correct it. And use real names for next steps. "Someone will follow up" is how follow-ups die.

Put the note where the work happens

A good decision block still fails if nobody can find it. People don't search a docs folder when they're confused by code. They look at the ticket, the PR, the commit or the file in front of them. So bring the decision there:

  • Paste the decision block into the ticket description, and link back to the full notes.
  • Quote the "Why" line in the PR description. Reviewers ask better questions when they know what was traded away.
  • Link the PR to the ticket. On GitHub, writing a keyword like "Fixes #412" links them, and when the PR merges into the default branch the issue closes automatically (GitHub Docs). Now anyone reading the code can walk back from the commit to the ticket to the meeting.
  • For architecture-heavy calls, write a short decision record in the repo. Nygard kept his as files under doc/arch/ and suggested one or two pages at most.

The exact tool doesn't matter much. What matters is that from the place where someone gets confused, they can follow links to the reason in one or two clicks.

Who this helps

The obvious winner is the new teammate from the opening. But the habit also helps the people who were in the room. When context lives next to the work, nobody has to be the team's living archive. The person who remembers every meeting can take a week off without getting pinged. GitLab's handbook makes the same point about agenda docs: they shift "the memorization burden away from humans."

It also makes disagreement healthier. When the reasons are written down, a teammate can challenge the decision on its merits ("the webhook has been stable for three months, can we revisit?") instead of on who made it.

Not every meeting needs this. A sync where nothing was decided needs a two-line summary at most. Save the decision block for meetings that changed what someone will build. If your team makes enough of those to lose track, a running decision log is the next step up, and the same idea works for checklists kept close to the work.

Try this week

  • Reserve the last five minutes of your next decision meeting for the five-line decision block.
  • Copy that block into the ticket it affects, with a link back to the full notes.
  • Quote the "Why" line in the PR description.
  • Pick one old decision people keep asking about and write its block retroactively, while someone still remembers.

After your next meeting, skip the "did someone take notes?" question. Ask where the decision lives now, and whether the person who needs it in two months will land on it from the code.

faqs.a: They don't need to be a transcript. Capture the key points and be clear on decisions and next steps. A short block works well: what was decided, why, which options were considered, when to revisit and who does what next.

Next to the work they affect. Paste the decision summary into the ticket, quote the reason in the pull request, link the PR to the ticket, and keep the full notes one click away. For architecture decisions, a short decision record in the repository works well.

faqs.q: Why do teams lose the reasons behind decisions?
faqs.a: Because the decision, the reasoning and the follow-up end up in different places: a chat thread, a meeting doc, a ticket. Months later, people either accept the decision blindly or reverse it blindly, as Michael Nygard put it in his post on architecture decision records.

faqs.q: Does every meeting need a decision block?
faqs.a: No. Use it for meetings that change what someone will build or how. A status sync where nothing was decided needs two lines at most.
